advisor.summary: The §41 research credit is the rare six-figure federal incentive open to ordinary product, software, and process businesses — and it is documentation-intensive in exact proportion to its value. Qualified research expenses (in-house wages, supplies, and 65% of contract research, domestic only) must clear the §41(d) four-part test at the business-component level, and most established claimants compute under the alternative simplified method: 14% of QREs over half the prior-three-year average, or 6% for first-time claimants with no history — precisely the math the engine runs. OBBBA restored immediate expensing of domestic research through new §174A, removing the amortization drag that distorted the credit decision from 2022 to 2024. §280C(c) then forces either a deduction add-back or the reduced-credit election, and qualified small businesses can point up to $500,000 of the credit at payroll tax. The exam environment punishes thin studies — Siemer Milling and Little Sandy Coal are the cautionary record — so the credit is only as strong as the experimentation file behind it.
mechanics: Qualified research expenses are in-house research wages, supplies consumed in research, and 65% of contract research payments, for domestic activities only; every claimed dollar must attach to a business component that passes the §41(d) four-part test — §174-eligible expenditures, technological in nature, aimed at a new or improved business component, with substantially all activity constituting a process of experimentation.

The engine computes the alternative simplified credit exactly: 14% of current-year QREs above 50% of the prior-three-year average, or 6% of all QREs when no prior-year history exists — the gross-credit figure before any §280C(c) adjustment.

§280C(c) requires either adding the credit back to income or electing the reduced credit on a timely-filed original return; because the model carries the gross number, the reviewer overlays the roughly 21% haircut (or the add-back) when presenting the net benefit.

OBBBA's §174A restored the immediate deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, with transition options for amounts capitalized in 2022–2024; foreign research stays on 15-year amortization under §174.

A qualified small business — under $5 million of gross receipts and no receipts before the five-year window — may elect under §41(h) to apply up to $500,000 of the credit against payroll taxes, monetizing the credit before any income tax liability exists.

Recent Form 6765 revisions add Section G business-component-level reporting, ending the era of single-number studies — optional for tax years beginning before 2026, mandatory for tax years beginning in 2026 and later (with carve-outs for qualified small businesses electing the payroll offset and for smaller claimants); the credit claim and its documentation now have to match at filing, not just on exam.

authority.note: The credit for increasing research activities — permanent, offering the regular and alternative simplified computation methods.
The four-part test and its exclusions (funded research, post-commercial-production work, adaptation, foreign research) — the ground where most overclaims die.
The qualified small business election to offset payroll tax, up to $500,000 — the monetization route for pre-profit companies.
No double benefit: a deduction add-back or the reduced-credit election on a timely-filed original return — the overlay the modeled gross credit needs.
OBBBA's restoration of immediate domestic R&E expensing via new §174A for tax years beginning after 2024, with 2022–2024 transition options; foreign R&E remains on 15-year amortization under §174.
The process-of-experimentation standard and the recordkeeping expectations examiners apply.

authority.cite: Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2019-37
authority.note: Credit denied where activities were described only in general terms with no documented experimentation — the cautionary tale on documentation.

authority.cite: Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)
authority.note: The substantially-all/process-of-experimentation requirement enforced quantitatively — shrink-back arguments will not rescue undocumented components.
Computation, the ASC and §280C elections, and the expanded business-component reporting on current revisions.

requirements: Domestic activities satisfying all four §41(d) prongs, identified and documented at the business-component level.
Contemporaneous substantiation: project lists, employee-level wage allocations, and experimentation evidence — design iterations, test logs, version histories.
A credible credit study mapping expenses to qualified activities — a percentage-of-payroll guess is an exam invitation, not a study.
The §280C(c) reduced-credit election made on the timely-filed original return, or the add-back computed.
For the payroll offset: qualified small business status verified and the §41(h) election made on Form 6765.
risks: The leading audit theory is the unsupported study: Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2019-37, denied credits where experimentation was asserted but never evidenced, and Little Sandy Coal extended the lesson to the substantially-all test — R&D claims also recur in IRS Dirty Dozen warnings about credit mills.

Funded research (customer- or grant-paid with rights or payment contingencies) and post-commercial-production refinement are the two most common overclaim categories, and both are categorically excluded.
Missing the §280C(c) election deadline forces the deduction add-back — generally the worse outcome for top-bracket pass-through owners.

The expanded Form 6765 Section G reporting exposes a thin study at filing — it was optional for tax years beginning before 2026 but is mandatory for most claimants in tax years beginning in 2026 and later; a claim that cannot name its business components should not be filed.
The credit is nonrefundable against income tax, with §39 carryovers the model does not track — sequence it against the client's actual liability.
stateNotes: Conformity: Missouri's rolling conformity picks up §174A expensing automatically, so the state deduction tracks the federal one; states that decoupled from federal research treatment need year-by-year checking for multistate clients.

PTET interaction: none directly — the federal credit passes to owners, while the slightly higher entity income from a §280C add-back (where elected against) flows into any pass-through entity tax base.

Missouri: the state's own qualified research expense credit (RSMo §620.1039, effective 2023) allows 15% of additional QREs — 20% when the research runs with a Missouri university — capped at $300,000 per taxpayer against a $10 million statewide pool; it is application-based through DED and exhausts early, so file the moment the window opens.
reviewChecklist: Four-part-test screening memo covers each claimed business component, with funded-research and post-commercial-production exclusions affirmatively ruled out.
Wage allocations tie to payroll records employee by employee, and experimentation artifacts exist for the largest components.
ASC versus regular method compared in the study; the modeled figure matches the chosen method's gross credit.
§280C(c) election status confirmed before filing, and the client sees the net-of-election benefit — not the gross model output.
Qualified small business payroll offset evaluated for eligible clients.
Missouri QRE credit application calendared where state QREs exist.

client.teaser: If your team designs, builds, tests, and improves things, part of that payroll can come back as a credit.
client.headline: Get paid back for solving hard problems
plainEnglish: If your business spends money making products, software, or processes better, the tax law rewards it. The reward is a credit, and it cuts your tax bill dollar for dollar. That is stronger than a deduction.

You do not need a lab or white coats. Manufacturers refining a process, contractors engineering around site problems, and firms building software often qualify. What matters is that your team solves technical problems by designing, testing, and refining.

The credit is only as good as its paper trail. The IRS pushes hard on big claims with thin files. So we build a real study: which projects qualify, whose time went in, and the records that prove it. Done right, it can repeat every year.
client.analogy: Think of it as a rebate on your problem-solving payroll: the government hands back part of what you already pay your team to figure things out.
benefits: Cuts your tax bill dollar for dollar, not just your taxable income
Rewards work you are already paying for
Newer companies can use it against payroll taxes before they owe income tax
Repeats every year the development work continues
steps: WE interview your team and pinpoint which projects truly qualify.
WE build the credit study, the wage allocations, and the documentation file.
YOU keep the project records we set up — test notes, versions, time tracking.
WE make the right elections and claim the credit on your return.
clientCommitments: Have your team keep the simple project records we set up — they are the audit defense
Tell us about customer-funded or grant-funded work so we exclude it correctly
Expect the credit to be reviewed — the study is built to be examined

annualMaintenance: Refresh the credit study each year — new projects in, completed or disqualified projects out
Update employee wage allocations and collect the year's experimentation artifacts
Confirm the §280C(c) election on each year's original return
File the Missouri QRE credit application when the DED window opens
deliverables: R&D credit study with business-component documentation
Employee wage allocation schedules tied to payroll
Form 6765 workpapers with the ASC computation and election record
Documentation kit for ongoing project record-keeping
